https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: 0:31 Footage shows NSW police officer boasting about 'punching' anti-Herzog protester in head – video New South Wales Footage of police officer boasting about punching Sydney anti-Herzog protester raises questions about conduct Male police officer caught on camera during 9 February protest against visit of Israeli president Isaac Herzog Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jordyn Beazley Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.36 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 06.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Video footage has emerged capturing a New South Wales police officer boasting about “punching” a protester in the head “when he was down”, before the protester was charged with assaulting police. Police body-worn camera footage, which was leaked to a social media account and widely shared over the weekend, reveals a male police officer telling his colleagues during the 9 February protest at Sydney town hall against a visit by the Israeli president, Isaac Herzog: “I fucking pumped that cunt.” A female officer can be heard replying, “So funny,” before the male officer says: “Then I punched him in the head when he was down.” NSW spent almost $500,000 on court cases lost against pro-Palestine protest groups Read more Guardian Australia understands the video relates to legal proceedings from a protester who was charged with assaulting police. They were one of three protesters who on Friday had the charges against them dropped. Police have now withdrawn charges against four of the 30 protesters charged in the wake of the protest. The three protesters who had their charges withdrawn on Friday were scheduled to face a joint hearing alongside 22 others in July 2027. The premier, Chris Minns, had previously urged the public “to not look at a 10-second clip without the full context” after a number of videos went viral showing police allegedly punching protesters and dragging Muslim worshippers away while they were praying. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The new video of the police bragging about punching the protester is understood to be the first bodycam footage to be widely shared publicly. In February, the independent police watchdog – the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (Lecc) – launched Operation Makalu to investigate allegations of police brutality at the protest. On Tuesday, the NSW Greens MP and spokesperson for justice, Sue Higginson, referred the leaked body-worn camera footage to the watchdog, alleging it was evidence of police misconduct. “The police misconduct that I personally witnessed on 9 February at town hall was obscene, the impunity was something I have not ever seen before and I have no doubt it was the result of the Minns Labor government suppressing protest with invalidly made laws,” Higginson said in a statement. “This footage shows the attitude of the police that night and should result in an immediate suspension and investigation of the officers involved. “The Lecc is already investigating the actions of the police that night, but this evidence warrants immediate action by the NSW police.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion A spokesperson for NSW police said they were aware of the video, but were unable to comment due to the ongoing Lecc investigation. Guardian Australia approached Minns for comment. The day after the protest, he said that the police were “put in an impossible situation” after protesters attempted to defy the public assembly restriction declaration (Pard) law, which police enforced during the protest. In April, the court of appeal found that law unconstitutional, ruling in favour of the Palestine Action Group and Blak Caucus who brought a challenge against it. Majed Kheir, a lawyer who represented two of the three protesters whose charges were on Friday withdrawn, said: “The withdrawal of a further three cases simply reflects recognition of the reality that these cases were doomed to fail. “The brutal conduct of police on 9 February plainly went so beyond the pale. All charges should be immediately dropped as a first step to restore some level of confidence in the NSW police force that our law enforcement institution can be accountable and acknowledge their wrongdoing.” A petition launched in June by the NSW Council for Civil Liberties calling for the charges against all the anti-Herzog protesters to be dropped has almost 3,000 signatures. Share this post Yesterday, we learned that the U.K. government’s solution — and I used that term loosely — is to hand asylum seekers a nine-page booklet that tells them that women are, in fact, human beings who have equal rights and that women must consent to sex. That’ll work as well as eating soup with a fork, of course. As I reported earlier, an Afghan illegal alien raped a woman in a London park while his Afghan illegal alien buddy held her date at knife point. Last year, two Afghan migrants raped a 15-year-old girl and went to court and said they didn’t know that women in the U.K. had rights and freedoms. Rather than stopping the import of backward-thinking men from misogynistic countries and deporting the ones who are already there, British politicians like Jess Phillips are pretending this issue isn’t specific to Muslim men , and insisting that all men are the problem and specifically called out Poland. I loathe this woman and everything and everyone associated with her. She smirks like everything is a big joke. She was a disgraceful minister with zero integrity and compassion. In this interview she condemns POLISH men… Poland – the safest county in Europe with the lowest rates… pic.twitter.com/2jUJwXNB29 — Orla Minihane (@orlaminihane) August 20, 2026 Poland records about 1,000 to 1,200 rapes per year; the U.K. recorded over 68,000 . But Polish men are the problem here? I don’t think so. Jess Phillips is the lowest of the low She’s deflecting from the migrant leaflets telling them not to rape children by saying ALL MEN need lessons in not raping women She shut down the Oldham Rape Gang Inquiry She lied about rape gang victims on the national inquiry She is in… — Basil the Great (@BasilTheGreat) August 20, 2026 “She is in the Government that continues to bring rapists to the shores of the UK,” the post reads. Recommended They just can’t help themselves. In Phillips’ world, it’s a worse crime to be a racist, or even perceived as racist, than it is to rape innocent British women and girls. Then again, Phillips might not want to admit her role in the scandal, either. Late in 2024, she refused to initiate a national public inquiry into the grooming gang exploitation, instead saying, “It is for Oldham Council alone to decide to commission an inquiry into child sexual exploitation locally.” In 2016, Phillips was the woman who downplayed the mass sexual assault of German women on New Year’s Eve 2015, saying, “A very similar situation to what happened in Cologne could be described as ‘Broad Street in Birmingham every week,” and saying Birmingham women are simply “baited and heckled” on their nights out. A couple of weeks ago, a Daily Mail columnist said it was “taboo” to talk about the rapes, and I said the U.K. had two paths forward: to deport these monsters and block future immigration or full-blown capitulation. I said then, and I say now, capitulation is the path they’re going to take. The pattern is now unmistakable. When Afghan asylum seekers rape women in London parks or claim ignorance of basic consent in British courts, the official response is a nine-page pamphlet. When the data and the victims point to cultural and demographic patterns that politicians find inconvenient, the response is to smear all men, specifically and especially the men from one of Europe’s safest countries, as the real problem. Jess Phillips has spent years perfecting this deflection: refusing a proper inquiry into the Oldham grooming gangs, dismissing survivor concerns, downplaying the mass sexual abuse of German women, and now lecturing the public that the issue is universal male entitlement rather than the deliberate importation of men from Third World countries that treat women as nothing more than property. It is not “racist” to notice that a country recording roughly 1,200 rapes a year is not the source of Britain’s crisis, while the British government continues to mass single, military-age men from Islamic nations and then thinks a leaflet about U.K. law means anything to them. Britain faces a choice that it can no longer ignore: protect British women and girls by stopping mass migration and deporting those who have already proven themselves a threat, or keep sacrificing them on the altar of tolerance and political correctness. Phillips and her colleagues have already chosen the second path. The rest us are under no obligation to follow them. The latest projections show the AfD on 44%, narrowly missing out on an absolute majority of seats in the state parliament in Magdeburg. However, the party has claimed a mandate to govern the state. "In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany," Tusk wrote. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement He said that "quite a few" have gathered in two opposition Polish parties - Confederation, and the former governing party Law and Justice (PiS). Reaction to the AfD's victory was more sympathetic elsewhere in Germany's neighbouring countries. The leader of the right-wing Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ), Herbert Kickl, described the result as a sign of political upheaval in Germany. "From today, the powerful wind of freedom from 1989 is blowing through Germany once again," said Kickl, drawing a comparison with the fall of the Berlin Wall. Voters in Saxony-Anhalt have torn down the "undemocratic firewall" against the AfD, according to Kickl. The FPÖ is Austria's largest party in parliament, but remains in opposition. Advertisement Advertisement Kickl said the AfD will "ultimately achieve its definitive breakthrough with Alice Weidel as Chancellor", said Kickl, referring to the party's national co-leader. In the Czech Republic, Parliament Speaker Tomio Okamura congratulated the AfD on its election success on public broadcasting channel CT. "Above all, I hope that it will form part of the new governing coalition in the federal state of Saxony-Anhalt," said Okamura, whose Freedom and Direct Democracy party is part of Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's government. This new app wants to give you a warning Zuckoff turns Bluetooth signals into a privacy alarm, offering people a way to know when camera-equipped smart glasses may be nearby. MC World Desk September 13, 2026 / 12:09 IST Zuckoff scans Bluetooth signals to detect nearby AI glasses. (Image credit: Unsplash) Zuckoff app detects smart glasses via Bluetooth. Helps users spot recording-capable AI glasses. Addresses privacy concerns with wearable cameras. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Smart glasses were supposed to make everyday technology less intrusive. Now, a new app is turning the tables by helping people spot the technology that could be watching them. Called Zuckoff, the iPhone app was created by Polish developer Pawel Szydlowski amid growing concerns about the privacy implications of camera-equipped AI glasses, particularly Meta’s Ray-Ban and Oakley models. The app scans Bluetooth signals emitted by compatible glasses and compares them with known device signatures to determine whether a pair may be nearby. The idea is surprisingly simple. Smart glasses need Bluetooth connectivity to communicate with phones and other devices, and those wireless signals can reveal information about the hardware. Szydlowski reportedly bought several models of smart glasses, studied their Bluetooth identifiers and built a database that Zuckoff can use for detection. The app then estimates proximity using signal strength. The timing is significant. Meta has increasingly promoted AI glasses as mainstream wearable technology, but their cameras have also raised questions about whether bystanders can tell when they are being recorded. Meta says its glasses feature a front-facing capture LED that signals when photos or videos are being captured, while its privacy guidance says the light is designed to indicate recording. Zuckoff, however, is not a magic privacy shield. Its detection does not establish that somebody is recording. It cannot identify the person wearing the glasses, determine exactly where the glasses are or intercept images, audio or video. A Bluetooth signal simply indicates that compatible hardware may be nearby. Related Stories Meta sued over AI smart glasses privacy after workers reviewed nudity, sex and other sensitive foota... Sarvam Kaze are the glasses PM Modi tried at the India AI Summit: Key features, availability, and mo... Meta could bring facial recognition to its Ray-Ban and Oakley smart glasses That limitation has not stopped interest. Reports say the app attracted around 5,000 users after its launch, while its developer has argued that people should at least have greater awareness of recording-capable devices around them. The app also offers background notifications through its paid Pro version. The bigger story may be what Zuckoff represents. As AI-powered wearables move from novelty products into public spaces, privacy protection is beginning to shift from something controlled entirely by manufacturers to something ordinary people can actively monitor. For now, Zuckoff offers only an early warning, not proof of surveillance. But its existence sends a pointed message to the smart-glasses industry: if wearable cameras are becoming ubiquitous, the people in front of those cameras may want a way to know they are there. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly.text: Figure caption, Watch: Videos show the al-Tubasi family's homes on fire and damage inside one of them before it was set ablaze By Yolande Knell Middle East correspondent ,Â Reporting from Jerusalem Published 4 hours ago More than 100 Israeli settlers have carried out attacks in a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank, stopping a family escorted by the Israeli military from returning to their homes, which had been seized weeks ago by settlers. Two houses belonging to the al-Tubasi family in Jalud, south of Nablus, were set on fire in the raid on Monday night and Israeli security forces were also targeted by settlers. Human rights groups say the events show how Israeli authorities are failing to take effective action against settler violence. "It was extremely terrifying, beyond words. It's hard to imagine the situation," Mahmoud al-Tubasi told the BBC. "My feeling now is that I am happy to have escaped death. I genuinely expected they were going to kill us." Al-Tubasi, 60, his wife Aida, 51, and their 33-year-old son, Wael, had returned to their properties accompanied by Israeli forces after Israel's High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed to go back. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Mahmoud al-Tubasi said he thought settlers were going to kill him and his family The family was forced to leave this summer after weeks of settler harassment and attacks. Extremist settlers had set up an illegal outpost close to Jalud and besieged three houses, including two belonging to the al-Tubasis' sons who are married with young daughters. Al-Tubasi said that he was called at about midnight and told that there was coordination with Israel's military for his family to go back to their houses. He received a message from Israeli officials saying that if he wanted to reclaim his property he had to go immediately with the army and Israeli border police. By torchlight, the family inspected one home. A video shared with the BBC shows that the settlers had already extensively damaged it - smashing holes through doors, tearing out electrical fittings, ripping up tiles, breaking windows and leaving rubbish strewn about. The toilet was smashed and appeared to be full of human waste. A large number of extremist settlers arrived in Jalud after alerts were posted in WhatsApp groups they use to coordinate action, saying that the Palestinian family they had forced out was returning and should be stopped. "As soon as we entered the house, which had already been completely destroyed, settlers started throwing stones at us. The army responded by firing tear gas at them, but there were so many settlers, more than 150, that the army could no longer control them," al-Tubasi told the BBC. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Israel's High Court has ruled that the al-Tubasi family must be allowed to return to their homes The grandfather says that a group of Israeli soldiers protected his family from the settlers who tried to approach them, using pepper spray to force them back. Settlers slashed the tyres of a military van they were put in and then they were transferred to an armoured military vehicle. As the family was being driven away, the settlers set fire to their car and both of their houses. Video shot from a distance shows smoke billowing from them. Al-Tubasi says that the Israeli security forces "essentially formed a barrier, took us out safely and got us away from there. But they did not take any action against the settlers themselves." An Israel Defense Forces (IDF) statement said that "more than 100 Israeli rioters were present in the village, blocking roads, setting tyres on fire, and throwing stones at security forces." The Israeli military said that three police officers were lightly injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged. It described the Tubasi family as victims of "nationalist crime" adding that "due to the violence, the mission to return the family to their home was not completed." The head of the local council in Jalud told reporters that residents had confronted the settlers leading to clashes which even spread to a nearby village, where a Palestinian woman was assaulted by settlers and her house set ablaze. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Israel's prime minister called on law enforcement authorities to prosecute those he called "rioters" One month ago, Aida al-Tubasi was attacked by masked Israeli settlers and injured along with American journalists who were interviewing her in Jalud. The high court decision, which criticised Israeli authorities for failing to crack down on settler violence, ruled that the family should be safely returned home by 20 September - more than a week ago. The legal ruling was strongly worded describing Israeli settlers' actions as "a completely unacceptable phenomenon that stands in contrast to the basic values and moral principles of the State of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he strongly condemned the attacks on security forces, calling on law enforcement, "to prosecute the rioters to the fullest extent of the law." Israeli police said that they had arrested three people suspected of being involved in the attacks. Speaking at the UN General Assembly last week, Netanyahu dismissed international concerns about settler violence. He accused the media of ignoring attacks on Jewish Israelis and covering "a handful of juvenile delinquents , about 150 in number, who throw stones, who chop down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires." According to the Israeli human rights group, Yesh Din, fewer than three per cent of police investigations into settler violence over the last two decades have led to a conviction. Ziv Stahl, its executive director, said the lack of effective law enforcement was because, "the violence is part of a systematic government policy aimed at pushing Palestinians out of the area and expanding Israeli control over land in the West Bank". Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank claiming biblical and legal rights to the land. Some ministers have said they aim to "bury the idea" that an independent Palestinian state could be set up in the territory along with East Jerusalem and Gaza. Settlements and outposts are illegal under international law. Levels of settler violence have reached an all-time high this year, according to the United Nations, which says that since 2023, more than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks and access restrictions in the occupied West Bank. In the same time period, the UN's Humanitarian Office (OCHA) has logged 6,199 attacks by Israeli settlers causing casualties or damage , external . According to OCHA, at least 82 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the West Bank this year and four Israelis have been killed - members of the security forces and civilians. At least 23 Palestinians were killed in the context of settler attacks. Photograph: Ukrainian Emergency Service/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv Ukrainian president tells US senators the delayed missiles have already been paid for by European countries, amid growing rift. What we know on day 1,700 Guardian staff and agencies Mon 19 Oct 2026 20.44 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US is deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine , deepening a public spat with Donald Trump. Speaking to US senators on Monday, the Ukrainian president claimed that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries under the prioritised Ukraine requirements list (Purl) program. According to Zelenskyy, the shipment is awaiting the signature of the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. A White House official, who spoke to the Washington Post on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy, said the US “continues to play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end”. Zelenskyy also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval. “All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down the support for us,” he said in remarks released by the Ukrainian presidency. The ‌Post reported the Trump ⁠administration ​had not approved ⁠the ⁠transfer of the interceptor ‌missiles ‌to Ukraine. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for soaring fuel prices that are a major issue in coming US midterm elections. “Maybe it’s time for ​Zelenskyy ‌to get ‌somebody else to negotiate” to end the war with Russia, Trump said on Monday. Zelenskyy said US decisions taken ⁠on the war – including delays in arms shipments and restrictions on ⁠intelligence sharing – were “hard ⁠to explain”. Washington denies making any changes to intelligence-sharing with Kyiv. Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Zelenskyy said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow. Ukrainian air force spokesperson Yuri Ihnat said on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv about 11pm, Andrew Roth reports. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike. Ukraine did receive a warning before a subsequent strike, Ihnat added. Zelenskyy said on social media on Monday morning: “Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners.” Six people, including young children, were killed when a Russian drone struck a park in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv region , authorities said. Zelenskyy decried a “pure atrocity”, saying on Facebook the drone “struck people directly – in a park near an ordinary cafe”, and a one-year-old girl was among those killed. The strike on Monday in Nova Vodolaga had also killed the girl’s mother. Trump’s ⁠envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway ​this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, Reuters quoted three people familiar with the matter as saying. Two of them said they expected Zelenskyy to ⁠attend the meetings. Another source said Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who was expected to take part in the talks, was sick and would attend virtually. The Oslo discussions were expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian prime ⁠minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the UK, France, Germany and Poland – the EU and Nato. Witkoff is also set ​to travel to Russia to meet Russian president Vladimir Putin, two sources said. The people, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the schedules were tentative and could change. Pope Leo has held a phone call with Zelenskyy , the Vatican said, and urged Ukraine and Russia to cooperate to let aid and ⁠food into the ⁠ blockaded town ​of Oleshky . Residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town have reported a deepening food crisis. The call ⁠on Monday came three days after the pontiff asked Putin to arrange a ceasefire so aid could enter Oleshky, a request the Kremlin did ⁠not address when it said Putin would help organise supplies.
